news.title: Gavin Newsom Reveals When He’ll Decide on 2028 Presidential Run
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said Thursday he expects to decide in early January whether to run for president in 2028, around the time his second term as governor ends.

“We’ll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January,” Newsom told Turkey’s state-run Anadolu news agency during a trip to Antalya for the United Nations climate summit.

Newsom had spoken about a possible White House run before, but until Thursday he hadn’t said when he’d make up his mind.

In a September interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, the governor said he would need the support of his wife and four children to run. Newsom is barred by California’s term limits from seeking a third term as governor. He also told Tapper he would sit out the race if former Vice President Kamala Harris sought the Democrat nomination.

“I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see,” Newsom said. “But I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

Fewer California voters are excited about a Newsom presidential run. A September poll from UC Berkeley’s Citrin Center and Politico found that 37% of registered voters in the state said they’d be excited about a Newsom bid, down from 48% in March. Harris’s numbers fell from 41% to 28% over the same period.

Newsom gave his January timetable a little more than a week after Democrats won control of the House and Senate. The party took Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa and Texas and picked up more than two dozen House districts, including some Trump had carried by double digits in 2024.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said Thursday he expects to decide in early January whether to run for president in 2028, around the time his second term as governor ends.

news.title: Democrat Ro Khanna Is Considering A Presidential Bid. He Could Be The Progressive Wing's Candidate.
news.text: California Congressman and Democrat Ro Khanna has said that, following the Democrats' landslide victory in the recent midterm elections, he is considering a presidential run in 2028."I'm certainly considering it, there are going to be bold progressives ... I'm going around the country, seeing whether the message will resonate ... I think that it's the president who sets the agenda for the party," Khanna is heard saying in response to a question about 2028 on video footage released by satellite television network C-SPAN on Friday.MSNOW reported similar news on Friday, stating that the Californian had told the outlet that he is "strongly considering" running for the Democrats' nomination and that he would "make a decision after the holidays."Khanna also noted that the midterm results made a 2028 bid "more likely than not," citing the victories of Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico and Scott Colom in the Michigan, Texas and Mississippi Senate races as evidence of the U.S. being "open to diversity ... open to people who are not part of the establishment."Khanna is not necessarily considered a frontrunner. According to a New York Times average of the last 15 polls on the Democrats' 2028 nominee, former presidential candidate Kamala Harris, California Governor Gavin Newsom, New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, as well as Mark Kelly and Pete Buttigieg, are leading the Democratic pack.Ocasio-Cortez, like Khanna, firmly belongs to the Democrats' progressive wing, and could command significant left-wing support.Nevertheless, Khanna's name recognition has been boosted significantly since the re-election of President Donald Trump to office.Khanna, alongside Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, was one of the leading sponsors of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, a bill that made files relating to the criminal activities of the late financier and convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein publicly available.The move made Khanna popular amongst progressives and wider sections of the American electorate.His wider economic vision also makes him a likely contender for the progressive camp heading into 2028; his self-described platform of "economic patriotism" proposes introducing a wealth tax on billionaires, guaranteeing "healthcare as a fundamental right, free and universal for every American," expanding child care access and funding of public schools and colleges as well as ending U.S. financial aid to Israel.In the immediate aftermath of the midterms, allies of Khanna's launched a committee, named "Run Ro," dedicated to laying the groundwork for the representative's presidential campaign if he decides to run.
news.summary: California Democrat Ro Khanna says he is considering a 2028 presidential campaign, citing recent Democratic victories and growing support for his progressive economic platform.

news.title: MAGA Is Scaring Away Republicans’ Most Loyal Voting Bloc
news.text:
Millions of evangelical Christian voters are abandoning Donald Trump in a massive warning that one of his most important power bases is eroding, a bombshell new analysis has found. 

The Washington Post has revealed that midterm election data from 343 counties with large concentrations of white evangelical voters show that voter turnout was just 66 percent of what it was in 2024. 

Data from the ACP Social Science Lab at Michigan State University shows that while Trump won in those areas by a margin of 62 points, Republican Senate candidates enjoyed just a 45-point advantage in this month’s election. 

Turnout in the heavily white evangelical counties was far lower than in nearby counties, where it was around 78 percent of its 2024 level, according to the Post. The low turnout likely played a key role in the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses, as Democrats seized control of the House and Senate and made inroads in traditionally deep-red states, including Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa, and others.

In typically ruby-red Mississippi, voters elected Democrat Scott Colom as the state’s first Black senator since the 19th century, signaling a shifting balance of power. 

“Those changes may have led to the Republican loss of the Mississippi U.S. Senate seat, surprising big Democratic margins in a few Senate races, and several Democratic pickups of GOP-held U.S. House seats around the country,” Dante Chinni, founder of ACP, told the Post.

White evangelicals have long been among the core elements of Trump’s MAGA movement, according to PRRI data. They backed Trump by 81 percent to 17 percent for Kamala Harris in 2024. 

But Trump’s policies are corroding his evangelical support, with voters concerned about the rising cost of living, the war with Iran, and allegations that Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself. A Pew Research survey ahead of the midterms found that while 78 percent of white evangelicals approved of the president at the start of his second term. That number has since dropped to 58 percent—a flashing red light for the Republican Party. 

In April, Trump deleted an AI-generated image depicting himself as a Jesus-like figure after it provoked a furious backlash from white evangelicals and other Christian communities. 

Trump’s support from white evangelicals had been bolstered in 2022 when Trump appointed justices to the Supreme Court who voted to overturn Roe v. Wade, long a key aim of the pro-life right.

news.title: Westerners Don’t Want Their Utilities Tied To California’s Power Market, Poll Shows
news.text:
A federal power agency is weighing whether to join a California-operated electricity market, but most Westerners polled say their utilities should stay independent.

A draft decision on which day-ahead electricity market the Bonneville Power Administration will join is expected in December, Bonneville senior spokesperson Kevin Wingert said in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation. The agency had proposed in March to join a rival to the California market, Markets+.

Seventy-two percent of adults surveyed in five Western media markets said their local utility should stay “independently governed.” Just 10 percent would rather see it coordinate with a “California-run system,” the council’s slides show. The remaining 19 percent said they were not sure.

Causeway Solutions ran the poll for the Western Energy Markets Integrity Council. The advocacy group opposes putting Bonneville’s federal hydropower in what it called a “California-centric trading platform.”

“Pushing these federal assets into the hands of California will have profound adverse consequences for affordability and reliability of power in a region that can ill afford it,” the council said in an Oct. 22 statement to the DCNF.

“The council is an independent not-for-profit organization that receives contributions from power providers and consumers, and individuals. It coordinates with other public interest groups,” Scott Segal, a Bracewell LLP partner speaking for the council, said in a statement. His statement did not name any of those contributors.

“It’s good for California. It’s just bad for everybody else that joins with them,” H. Sterling Burnett, director of the Arthur B. Robinson Center on Climate and Environmental Policy at the Heartland Institute, told the DCNF in a Tuesday interview.

When the DCNF asked who would get power if the whole West ran short, Burnett said, “Well, the big dog eats first.”

He compared it to fights over the Colorado River, saying California gets the most water when there are shortages.

“They have the representatives in the House. They have the biggest population. They get it first,” Burnett said of California.

“California’s disastrous energy policies should serve as a warning to every Western state and no state should allow Sacramento to export its failures across state lines,” Oliver McPherson-Smith, vice chair for energy and environment policy at the America First Policy Institute, said in a statement to the DCNF.

“Customers in other Western states have good reason to resist putting their electricity bills and reliability under the influence of California politicians they didn’t elect and cannot hold accountable,” Jason Isaac, founder and CEO of the American Energy Institute, said in a statement. “Accountability should stay with the people who pay the bills.”

“The Department of Energy is committed to ensuring that American families and businesses, including those across the Pacific Northwest, have access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity,” a department spokesperson said in a statement to the DCNF.

“Markets+ provides independent governance today,” the Southwest Power Pool, which would run Markets+, said in a statement. “More than one market in the West promotes choice and competition, which enables better outcomes for all participants and states.”

The California Independent System Operator did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment. (RELATED: Data Center Boom Sparks Battle Over Power Costs, New Regulations)

Independence came out ahead in each market. Support ran from 64 percent in the Billings, Montana, area to 81 percent in the Tri-Cities of Washington.

Those two results carry margins of error of 4.7 points in Billings and 4.9 points in the Tri-Cities, per the slides.

Among the 1,733 people who picked a side, 88 percent chose independence and 12 percent favored coordinating with California.

Eighty-four percent of those surveyed were at least somewhat worried about their electric bills.

Causeway surveyed 2,095 adults, not registered voters, from Sept. 21 to 25 in the Boise, Idaho; Tri-Cities, Washington; Medford, Oregon; Gilbert and Mesa, Arizona; and Billings, Montana, media markets, the council’s polling page says. The text-to-web survey has an overall margin of error of 2.1 percentage points.

Bonneville’s March proposal set a target start date of Oct. 1, 2028, for Markets+. That came after a May 2025 Bonneville policy that put the agency on a path toward Markets+.

That plan is now under review. Bonneville Administrator and CEO Travis Kavulla wrote in a Sept. 3 letter that he had committed to reviewing that course “with fresh eyes.”

He would propose a change in Bonneville’s next draft decision if the agency sees “concrete actions” on governance of the California operator’s market, he wrote. Independent board leadership topped his list.

California revised its laws in 2025 so a separate regional body could govern that market with a board “appointed through an independent process rather than by state actors,” Kavulla noted.

That body, the Regional Organization for Western Energy, is set to interview candidates for its first CEO in December, RTO Insider reported Nov. 11.

“A more unified grid in the West with greater scale, market depth, and more contiguous corridors may alleviate operational and economic risks that would persist in a more fragmented market footprint,” Wingert, Bonneville’s senior spokesperson said. (RELATED: ‘Whole ’Nother Rent’: Soaring Electricity Prices In Kamala Harris’ Home State Are Crushing Residents)

Size is the draw. Leaving out Bonneville’s balancing area, the California operator’s market averaged 39 gigawatts of net generation, against 19 for Markets+. Kavulla cited federal Energy Information Administration data.

The Southwest Power Pool’s website lists an address in Little Rock, Arkansas.

Lawmakers from the Southwest Power Pool’s home state want Bonneville to stay the course. Republican Arkansas Sens. Tom Cotton and John Boozman wrote to Kavulla on Sept. 25 backing Bonneville’s “timely participation” in Markets+.

“The importance of independent governance cannot be overstated,” they wrote. The senators added that the California operator “is and remains statutorily beholden to the interests of the State of California.”

Western Montana’s electric co-op managers said in an Oct. 1 letter to Kavulla that their co-ops “strongly favor SPP.”

Advanced Energy United, which represents clean energy businesses, backed Bonneville’s review in September. The group’s senior director, Brian Turner, said the agency “recognizes the important strides that have been made around governance,” Utility Dive reported.

Bonneville has a workshop on its choice scheduled for Nov. 19, Wingert said.

Kavulla asked the regional body to adopt a framework that lets market participants “initiate and evaluate major market proposals,” with the end of November as his target.
news.summary: ‘It’s good for California. It’s just bad for everybody else that joins with them’

news.title: Democrats' midterm gains pose fresh challenges for Trump and Republicans: Report
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 14 (IANS) With Democrats holding majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, growing discontent with President Donald Trump is likely to make negotiations with the executive difficult, raising the prospect of prolonged policy paralysis in the United States, a report has said. The Democrat-controlled legislature is also expected to intensify scrutiny of Trump's decisions and his family's financial dealings. Meanwhile, the possibility of impeachment is once again gaining traction in the media, Sanjay Pulipaka, Chairperson of think tank 'Politeia Research Foundation', wrote in India Narrative. “In the Senate, the Democratic Party controls about 54 seats, while the Republican Party holds 44. In the House of Representatives, the Democrats won about 254 seats, while the Republicans won about 162. The Democrats won not only in swing states such as Georgia, Michigan, New Hampshire, and North Carolina, but also in Republican strongholds such as Iowa, Kansas, Texas, and even South Carolina. The scale of anti-incumbency is evident in the fact that, after a few decades, Texas has elected a Democratic senator and a Democratic governor, and Kansas has elected its first Democratic senator since 1932,” Pulipaka noted. “What explains the electoral outcome? It appears that the Iran war has proved to be very costly for the Republican Party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump promised ‘no more wars.’ However, while the intervention in Venezuela turned out to be brief, the Iran War proved to be a different ball game altogether. In fact, Vice President J D Vance noted that the Iran War led to the midterm electoral defeat," he added. According to the report, the Republican Party will reassess its approach after aligning with Trump's agenda before the midterm elections in view of his popularity and electoral success. With Trump's governing style and political approach increasingly proving costly, it said, the Republican Party may reconsider its association with his agenda. Republican leaders with presidential ambitions are reportedly weighing the option of distancing themselves from the Trump administration. The report noted that for the Democratic Party, the challenge now lies in consolidating its gains among voters who have traditionally aligned with the Republicans but recently voted for the Democrats. Its ability to retain these voters remains uncertain, particularly if it reverts to a hardline position on cultural issues, potentially driving them back to the Republican fold. The party's agenda will depend on a new generation of prominent leaders and possible presidential candidates, including Andy Beshear, Gavin Newsom, James Talarico, JB Pritzker, Jon Ossoff, Josh Shapiro, Pete Buttigieg and others, the report mentioned. “Established leaders such as Barack Obama, Rahm Emanuel, Kamala Harris and others should nudge the young leaders to adopt a more prudent strategy. They will have to take note of the fact that many Democrats, such as Senator-elect Talarico (Texas), Senator-elect Adam Hamilton (Kansas) and others, have campaigned ‘around Christian faith and court a segment of voters who had drifted towards Republican’,” India Narrative stated. “The Republicans may have lost this election, but for Democrats to win the Presidential election in 2028, agenda-setting will play a critical role,” it added.

news.title: Biden left Ireland feeling he could ‘be elected president’ here after 2023 visit
news.text:
Former US president Joe Biden has said he left Ireland feeling he could be “elected president” here after his State visit in 2023. 

In extracts from his upcoming memoir Promise Me, America, to be published on November 17th, Biden said the visit “restored my soul and revived my spirit”.

He wrote: “The trip had restored my soul and revived my spirit, which I’d needed. I knew I was headed home for the fight of my political life. 

“I left feeling I could be elected president in Ireland. Now I was about to find out if I could be reelected president in the United States.”

Biden dropped out of the race for the White House the following year after a disastrous debate performance against Donald Trump. He then backed his vice president, Kamala Harris, who secured the Democratic nomination before losing to Trump in 2024. 

Biden also recalled a chance meeting with Fr Frank O’Grady at Knock Shrine. Fr O’Grady, then the US army chaplain at Walter Reed Medical Centre, performed the last rites sacrament on his son Beau Biden, who died of brain cancer in 2015.

“The sight of him brought tears to my eyes,” Biden wrote. 

Biden also said he has good memories of his address at St Muredach’s Cathedral in Ballina on April 14th, 2023, in front of 27,000 “wildly enthusiastic” people. 

“The trip was an emotionally resonant one for me.”

[ Hunter Biden: My father beat Trump ‘like a drum’Opens in new window ]

Looking back on the G7 summit in Cornwall, England, in 2021, Biden discussed his anger with Brexit. 

“Brexit threatened to undermine the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, which had done so much good in bringing peace to Northern Ireland. That was important to me, as a proud Irish American. 

“I also disapproved of Brexit for its ultranationalist claims, and for making many promises that could not possibly be kept.”

He believed “populist leaders and opportunists” had “sold the British people out” by backing Brexit. 

However, he said he “preferred to work out our differences in private”, particularly because former UK prime minister Boris Johnson was the host of the event. 

In another notable section, Biden reveals his admiration for the late Queen Elizabeth, despite being on record about his Irish American mother’s anti-English sentiment. 

[ Civil liberties group criticises Garda response to Joe Biden protest at TrinityOpens in new window ]

He also said the queen reminded him of his mother. 

“She and I had a natural rapport, which might have surprised my mother, to put it mildly. Mom’s Irish blood made it difficult for her to admire the British crown, and she remembered historical grievances as if she had experienced them personally. 

“In fact (I can’t believe I’m about to say this), the queen’s steely strength, combined with the glint of humour in her eye, reminded me of no one as much as Catherine Eugenia Finnegan.” 

Biden has often spoken about his admiration for Irish literature and poetry, including the works of Seamus Heaney. 

He reveals he took inspiration from James Joyce in his 2020 inaugural address. 

“In my first letter, I had shared some words attributed to James Joyce: ‘When I die, Dublin will be written on my heart.’ I returned to them here. Because of you, Delaware will forever be written on my heart. I’ll see you back home.”
news.summary: Former US president remembers his trip to Ireland in several passages in his upcoming memoir Promise Me, America

news.title: The 2028 presidential race is already full of surprises, prediction markets say
news.text: The 2028 presidential election seems far away. Or is it already here? The midterm ballots are barely counted, and a long list of would-be candidates is already elbowing for a lane in a campaign that, by Election Day, will feel like it started during the Truman administration. Outside the Super Bowl, few things are as popular on prediction markets as a presidential race. Two years before anyone casts a ballot, Kalshi's 2028 markets have already drawn nearly half a billion dollars in trading. While prediction markets have an excellent long-term record of accuracy, this far from an election, you can't expect surgical precision. STU BURGUIERE: PUT YOUR MONEY WHERE YOUR MOUTH IS: PREDICTION MARKETS WON THE MIDTERMS What the markets can show us is who's trading like a blue chip, who's stuck in the middle, and whose campaign feels like a penny stock that needs a miracle rally to be competitive. So let's look ahead with a way-too-early presidential market report, starting at the top. The blue chips What if I told you the Democratic front-runner for 2028 is a man a third of Democrats have never heard of? That's what a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found when it comes to Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, and plenty of other Americans are drawing a blank too. Still, a Democrat who wins Georgia by 18 points, in a state President Trump carried in 2024, doesn’t stay anonymous for long. Kalshi gives him a 26% chance of winning the Democratic nomination, the best in the field. Not bad for a guy much of his own party couldn't pick out of a lineup. NEW POLL COMPLICATES VANCE’S STATUS AS TRUMP’S LIKELY 2028 HEIR APPARENT On the Republican side, Vice President J.D. Vance leads the pack, with a 33% chance of winning the nomination but only a 12% chance of winning the presidency. That gap fits what election analyst Nate Silver calls the VP curse. Vice presidents whose bosses are underwater in the polls tend to win their party’s nomination, then lose in November. Then again, Vance has been underestimated before, and he seems to be at his best in high-leverage situations. Both men have also hinted they might not run at all. Coming from politicians, that promise has roughly the credibility of a vow of celibacy from Jensen Huang. The mid-caps California Gov. Gavin Newsom looked like a blue chip a year ago. His chance of winning the Democratic nomination has since cratered from 37% to about 12%. He leaves office in January, which frees him up for a full-time campaign and gives even more airtime to a man who has never been accused of camera shyness. Whether voters want that is another question. AOC TAPS POWER PLAYER WHO HELPED BERNIE SANDERS DEFY THE ODDS AS MAJOR 2028 DECISION LOOMS Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez sits around 13% to win the Democratic nomination. The bigger question is which race she's running in. Traders actually think she's more likely to run for the Senate than for president. Either way, somebody is going to claim the democratic socialist lane. If it's not her, maybe Bernie Sanders takes a third crack at it. He'll only be 87. Like Ocasio-Cortez, Secretary of State Marco Rubio faces a which-job question. He's at 18% to win the Republican nomination, and the market sees him as just as likely to be the running mate as the nominee. VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ran in 2024 and also leaves office in January, has been the biggest riser in the Republican market since the midterms. He was under 5% to win the nomination before the votes were counted and is now at 17%, nipping at Rubio's heels. The penny stocks Then come the penny stocks. On the Democratic side, that's a crowd in the single digits for the nomination: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Former Vice President Kamala Harris lands here too, a somewhat embarrassing showing for the woman at the top of the ticket two years ago. If you're shopping the bargain bin, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore at 2.2% and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at 0.7% might be in your wheelhouse. (In dead last, at 0.0%: Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz.) Josh Hawley could be value plays. And somewhere in that mix is President Donald Trump, who I wouldn't put past publicly flirting with a constitutionally prohibited third run just to annoy the media. The long-term outlook Many of these names won’t make it to the first primary. Today’s penny stock could be next summer’s blue chip. news.title: Democrats may have found a way around the Electoral College
news.text:
The 2026 midterms were a drubbing for Republicans at nearly every level of government. But there’s an overlooked upshot of the Democrats’ sweep that could effectively alter the U.S. Constitution and the way the country elects its president.

The National Popular Vote Compact is now easily achievable.

I cannot overstate the seismic shift that the NPVC will bring to presidential elections

The NPVC is an agreement among states to assign their Electoral College votes to whoever wins the most votes nationwide in a presidential election, regardless of which candidate wins the most votes in the state. It goes into effect only if enough states join, through state legislation, to ensure the compact states will anoint the winner. Hence the states in the compact must have collectively 270 or more Electoral College votes.

The compact is also a partisan issue — Democrats support it; Republicans oppose it. Until the morning of November 4, the NPVC was stuck at 222 Electoral College votes.

However, with Democrats gaining lawmaking authority — i.e., control of both houses of the state legislature and governorship — in Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Nevada, the NPVC has a clear shot of controlling the outcome of the 2028 election.

If the five newly Democrat-controlled states pass compact legislation, the NPVC will reach 283 Electoral College votes. Any one of Arizona, Wisconsin, or Nevada could not pass NPVC legislation, and the compact will still go into effect.

I cannot overstate the seismic shift that the NPVC will bring to presidential elections, nor ignore the significant constitutional questions it raises.

The NPVC will make every vote cast in every hamlet, town, and metropolis have equal influence in the final tally for president. Traditional swing-state-based electoral strategy will be useless — the goal for presidential campaigns will be to turn out every voter that they can everywhere in the country.

From a democracy perspective, it sounds great. “Every vote equal” is the rallying cry for the NPVC movement. It is not an unalloyed good, though. For folks skeptical of money in politics, the NPVC makes campaigning drastically more expensive.

Take, for example, the closest thing we’ve had to two parties competing on a national scale for every possible vote: the 2026 midterms. Democrats and Republicans actually tried to win every Senate contest, and the result was the most expensive election in American history: close to $12 billion spent.

The high for presidential elections, in 2020, is just over $6 billion, because whole swaths of the country — the South, the Northeast, the Pacific Coast — are uncontested. And the newly opened battlegrounds will be in some of the most expensive places to campaign: New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, Dallas, and so on.

RELATED: The GOP’s old dogs had better learn some new tricks

 Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Presidential elections under the NPVC will look a lot more like midterms, and given the higher stakes, the country could easily see more than $20 billion spent for a single office. Presidential election spending will finally catch up with potato chip spending (about $25 billion per year).

In addition to spending, the NPVC raises some thorny legal questions.

Right now, the national popular vote is a fiction calculated by summing 51 separate jurisdictions’ final vote tallies. But each state gets to its final tally in a different way. Some are all mail ballots, others have longer or shorter early voting, and so on. So a vote in Oregon doesn’t really mean the same thing as a vote in Florida.

That’s a significant, nationwide equality problem for the NPVC.

Additionally, since states shifted to awarding their Electoral College votes to the statewide winner in the 1830s, Americans expect their vote to translate to their state’s influence on the outcome. Under the NPVC, each state’s voters lose their unique impact on who becomes president.

For example, think of yourself as an Indian-American voter in California who had the opportunity to express, through California’s electoral votes, your preference for the first candidate of Indian descent, Kamala Harris. With the NPVC, you can’t do that any more, because California’s Electoral College votes would have gone to Donald Trump in 2024.

So the five states that have shifted to unified Democrat control should carefully consider whether they want to join the NPVC. While attractive from an abstract perspective, the compact has significant flaws and downsides.

If the states do join, though, 2028 will be an objectively historic election.

news.title: Democrats Won Congress. Can Their Leaders Read the Room? | Opinion
news.text: Democrats have won back Congress. Whether the party's established leadership understands what brought them there is another matter. The November 3 midterms dealt President Donald Trump a sweeping rebuke. Democrats captured both chambers, won Senate races in traditionally Republican states and regained much of the support lost in 2024. Yet barely a week later, attention has shifted to Senate Leader Chuck Schumer and House Leader Hakeem Jeffries, amid growing calls for new leadership and an incoming congressional class willing to challenge the party's assumptions about economic inequality, health care, corporate influence and American foreign policy. The results deserve careful interpretation. According to the Associated Press Voter Poll, about seven in 10 voters under 30 supported Democratic House candidates, compared with a roughly even split between Trump and Kamala Harris in 2024. Hispanic voters, Black men, moderates and lower-income Americans also moved toward Democrats. This was a broad rejection of Republican governance, not an exclusive endorsement of the progressive left. But it would be equally mistaken to assume voters wanted a return to the Democratic politics of the past. Young voters were particularly concerned about the cost of living and the war with Iran. Many voted out of frustration with economic insecurity and military intervention rather than party loyalty. Their support cannot be taken for granted, especially after a generation that moved toward Trump in 2024 shifted decisively away from him two years later. The newly elected Democrats reflect these changing expectations. Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former public health official, became the first Muslim elected to the United States Senate after defeating Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan. James Talarico won in Texas, challenging Christian nationalism while emphasizing economic inequality. Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Troy Jackson in Maine are among the other incoming senators bringing different constituencies and priorities to Washington. Their arrival coincides with the departure of longtime Democratic figures including Nancy Pelosi, Steny Hoyer, Jerry Nadler and Jan Schakowsky, while other incumbents have lost primaries to younger challengers. But age is hardly the central issue. Bernie Sanders remains one of the oldest figures in American politics and one of the most influential among younger progressives. The dispute concerns political direction, not birth dates. That dispute has reached the party's leadership. A petition opposing Jeffries as the next House speaker has attracted more than a million signatures, although he retains substantial support within the caucus, including from prominent progressives. Schumer faces a more direct challenge. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is considering a leadership bid, and El-Sayed has said he would support him. Schumer nevertheless retains considerable backing, and his role in helping Democrats regain the Senate cannot be dismissed. The disagreement is not over confronting Trump. Jeffries has already signaled aggressive congressional oversight. The larger question is whether Democrats will reconsider policies that have divided the party for years. Economic policy is one test. El-Sayed campaigned on Medicare for All, affordability and curbing corporate influence. He has long warned against embracing the rhetoric of universal health care while abandoning single-payer reform, highlighting the tension between ambitious promises and incremental compromise. With millions struggling to afford health care, housing and everyday necessities, moderates emphasize fiscal discipline, broad coalitions and practical compromises. Progressives argue that excessive caution has left structural problems unresolved. The election settled neither dispute. Democrats must now show they can deliver results. Foreign policy may prove even more contentious. In an NPR interview after his victory, El-Sayed welcomed Trump's announced intention to end American military assistance to Israel and called for an end to sales of weapons used in Gaza, where leading experts have concluded that genocide has occurred. He also questioned American military support for countries including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Pakistan, arguing that public resources should instead support health care, schools and infrastructure at home. He called for equal rights and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis and greater consistency in applying international law. His willingness to agree with Trump on a specific policy while rejecting his broader agenda challenges a political culture in which positions are too often judged by who advances them rather than their merits. It also exposes a longstanding Democratic divide. Much of the party's leadership has treated support for Israel as a settled foreign policy commitment, even as younger voters, progressives and some elected officials increasingly question unconditional military assistance. The destruction and killings in Gaza deepened that divide, while the war with Iran has raised further questions about military intervention, congressional authority and the costs of American foreign policy. These questions cannot be avoided, nor should disagreement over Israel be reduced to accusations about religion or political loyalty. El-Sayed's victory, despite repeated attacks on his Muslim faith and views on Israel, challenges the assumption that Muslim candidates must mute their convictions to win statewide office. Not every voter necessarily agreed with him, but his election demonstrates that such positions need not be politically disqualifying. Congress has constitutional authority over spending, war and executive oversight. Democratic control of both chambers beginning in January offers an opportunity to investigate abuses, scrutinize military operations and demand accountability grounded in evidence and constitutional principle rather than political retaliation. The Democrats' new coalition includes progressives, moderates, younger and working-class voters, and Americans motivated primarily by opposition to Trump. Their differences are real, and a party seeking to govern must accommodate disagreement without treating dissent as disloyalty. Established leaders bring experience, institutional knowledge and the ability to assemble legislative majorities. But those strengths become liabilities when experience hardens into resistance to change. Replacing Schumer or Jeffries would not resolve the party's divisions, just as retaining them need not prevent reform. What matters is whether Democrats can move beyond opposing Trump to address the economic and foreign policy disagreements within their own coalition. Voters have changed the composition of Congress. Whether they can change the Democratic Party remains to be seen. Faisal Kutty is a professor of law at Southwestern Law School, affiliate faculty at the Rutgers Center for Security, Race and Rights, a regular contributor to the Toronto Star and a contributing editor for the Washington Report on Middle East Affairs. The views expressed in this article are the writer's own.

news.title: As Democrats win big, thirst traps of male candidates take social media by storm
news.text:
If you're on social media, there's a good chance you've seen the videos: people getting hot and bothered about the young men Democrats just elected.

"I'm looking at you, Rob Sand. I'm looking at you, Jon Ossoff. I'm looking at you, El-Sayed," said fitness coach Jesse Barton, reacting to the midterm results. "I am looking, I am not the only one, and I'm very happy about what I see."

There are debates over candidates' relative levels of hotness. There are a lot of AI-generated images. And there are many, many montages of the politicians set to sexy pop music.

One of the most viral pieces of content was a parody Tiger Beat magazine cover featuring Democratic men … which Manoushka Guerrier, an LA-based chef and content-creator, took one step further.

"I created the entire Tiger Beat style personality quiz, complete with the different boy band personas," she said. The quiz gives people matches including "the Babyface" (Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico) and "the Heartthrob" (Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel).

Guerrier pays a lot of attention to politics, and she emphasizes that these guys' looks are just a bonus.

"They're young and they're ballsy and they're smart, and they're not just smart; they're brilliant," she says.

The tidal wave of attention on these young men creates a striking contrast to the first Trump midterm, in 2018. That election — after the Women's March, Me Too and the long list of assault and misconduct allegations against President Trump — yielded a record-setting wave of Democratic women. It all suggests that the thirsty social media posts aren't just a cheeky trend; they also say a lot about how Democrats have responded to the Trump era.

A response to Trump

Two main forces are behind the wave of attention on these men according to Christina Wolbrecht, a political science professor at Notre Dame University.

"I think it's a function of our kind of society-wide debate about masculinity," she said. "And I also think it's about age."

The age side is straightforward — just ahead of the midterms, a majority of likely voters said they favored candidates with new ideas over those with experience in the job, according to a NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll.

The masculinity side, meanwhile, is in response to MAGA and its elevation of a very specific type of manhood, Wolbrecht said.

"For 10-plus years, Donald Trump has presented one very distinct version of masculinity," she said. "It's very much power over [others]. It's very much power through wealth and status."

Manliness took center stage on the Democratic side this election. Candidates leaned into it, with people like Rutinel and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed posting weightlifting videos. El Sayed at one point did a video spoofing Love Island.

Voters noticed, posting admiring videos well before the election. Meanwhile, the media noticed and amplified this narrative, with profiles and think pieces throughout the midterm cycle, and reporting on Democrats' "rugged" and "authentic" candidates.

'That's a girly thing to be, is a Democrat'

Amplifying young, "manly" men may have boosted the party in this election. That's because Democrats had a problem after Kamala Harris lost the presidency in 2024, according to Democratic strategist Monica Venske.

"The feeling within the straight male demographic, if you will, [was] that it just wasn't cool to be a Democrat," she said. "It wasn't sexy to be a Democrat. It's not manly to be a Democrat. That's a girly thing to be, is a Democrat."

That's why she started the Instagram account Boyfriends We Deserve, where she highlights attractive Democrats — mostly men, but a few women as well.

Venske explains she is careful in how she posts about women's looks — unlike when she talks about men, like Montana's incoming Democratic congressman.

"Like when I call Sam Forstag hot, it will most likely never, ever hurt him," she said. "But I can call someone like Keisha Lance Bottoms hot and that could hurt her every time."

She said she instead will call the women "baddies" or focus on their hair, as opposed to highlighting their bodies or overall looks.

To Venske, the Boyfriends We Deserve posts are part of making it clear that the Democratic party is a big tent that includes young men.

"I'm like, 'Look at all these manly guys who are Democrats,'" she said. "Sam Forstag is an example I usually give. He was like a smokejumper in Montana. And in his announcement video for Congress, he's fixing up a truck. If a guy who is jumping out of planes to put out fires and fixing up trucks can be a Democrat, you can be a Democrat, I promise."

…But Democratic women won, too

All of that said, plenty of Democratic women ran and won this year, including several historic firsts: Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms, for example, will be the first Black woman governor. New Mexico's Deb Haaland will be the first Native American woman governor. Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan will be the nation's first Native American woman senator.

That highlights a big difference between this midterm and 2018's wave of women.

Since that election, Democrats have seen Joe Biden defeat Trump, and then watched a second woman lose the presidency to Trump. And while Democrats most certainly do still elect women — far more than Republicans — the masculinity of their male candidates received outsized attention this year.

It's possible, then, that the attention on Democratic men isn't simply lighthearted, but is part of Democrats' continual conversation about electability.

"I hear it from all sorts of people with all sorts of engagement that 2016 and 2024 proved that it took old-guy, aviator sunglasses Joe Biden to defeat Trump," Wolbrecht said, "and we need more of that and not more Kamala Harrises or Hillary Clintons."

"I think that's a mistake," she added quickly. "I think it's a misunderstanding of what happened in '16 and in '24. But the meaning we put on elections has consequences and it really shapes what parties do strategically going forward."

Democrats have struggled to win over men in recent elections. For example, Harris won 43 percent of men overall in 2024. This year, the party won 50 percent of the men's vote.

Guerrier disagrees that the attention on candidates' looks is about electability, but she thinks that for a lot of voters, this election was about changing the Democratic Party's story.

"It was just like these guys came out of nowhere, and it was just so refreshing that, wow, we can get out of this darkness and into something that is hopeful," she said.
news.summary: It's everywhere on social media: Democrats celebrating the attractive men voters elected in the midterms. But it's bigger than a meme and says a lot about politics of masculinity in the age of Trump.
news.author: Danielle Kurtzleben

news.title: Trump just made JD Vance’s path to the White House harder
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s frequent social media sign-off, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, has become as much a part of his trademark style as his make-up and hairdo. It’s more comic than sinister.

However, when Trump told Vice-President JD Vance on Truth Social to “focus his complete and total attention” on investigating alleged fraud in Democratic cities rather than waste his time on a deal with Iran, concluding it with TYFYATTM was a way of telling him to shut up about Iran or face his wrath.

This order to stay in his lane puts Vance in a lose-lose situation. The Memorandum of Understanding he negotiated with Iran in June is dead. He has been stripped of any further peace-brokering role. If Trump says, “Don’t mention the war,” Vance can’t even voice his opinion on it as part of his delicate bid for the 2028 nomination, but has to leave it to surrogates to make the case for him.

As for investigating corruption in Democrat-run cities, that’s about as desirable a task as the one former President Joe Biden gave his vice-president Kamala Harris on immigration. If you remember, the luckless Harris was supposed to address the “root causes” of immigration when the primary one was Biden’s own border policies.

Good luck, Vance, persuading voters to “look over there” at evidence of welfare fraud in Minneapolis, when Congress will start poring over alleged crimes and misdemeanours by the Trump family and their allies as soon as the new blue wave of lawmakers take their seats in January. He will need all the skills of a magician to pull that one off.

“Donald Trump and JD Vance are attempting to gaslight and distract the American people from noticing the rampant corruption happening right under their noses at the White House,” Kendall Whitmer said on behalf of the Democratic National Committee. “Trump, his kids, and his administration have made billions off their access to the White House.”

Now that Vance has been muzzled, I wonder whether we will ever see him again at the podium in the role of surrogate White House press secretary, since Trump obviously doesn’t trust him to deliver the right message. This is despite the fact that the President remains sorely in need of a replacement for his favourite sparrer with the media, Karoline Leavitt. After some comedy knockabout, it turned out that Trump’s great mate, UFC chief Dana White, wouldn’t touch her job with a bargepole.

However, the behind-the-scenes spinning wars have begun in earnest over whether Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be the preferred 2028 candidate from within the Trump administration. Let’s just say it’s remarkable how quickly Rubio emerged in the New York Times as the hero of the Nvidia sex-and-spy scandal, having reportedly briefed the President back in May about Jensen Huang’s alleged misdeeds. (Trump has said, “No, I didn’t hear about it then.”)

By the same token, the Washington Post has just revealed that the clean-cut Rubio spent $1.2 million of taxpayers’ money on military jet flights to watch his son play American football for his college team in Florida, despite his son being a “walk-on” who mostly stays on the bench (the Secretary of State is required to travel by government plane). The university stadium, the paper reported, is known as “The Swamp”. The timing feels significant.

Vance’s friends and rivals have also been busy. Thus a report on CNN this week claimed that the Vice-President was giving “serious consideration to not running for President in 2028” at virtually the same time as Politico reported “Vance sees an opening in the post-election blame game.”

Andrew Kolvet, executive producer of The Charlie Kirk Show podcast, claimed Vance’s opposition to the Iran war would work in his favour. “I think JD warmly welcomes that fight, because he not only has the moral high ground but also the wildly more popular position,” he said. An anonymous friend added, “JD’s critics are doing the job for him.”

Neither Vance nor Rubio have confirmed they will run. Rubio has remained especially tight-lipped. “I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore. I just won’t do it,” he recently said.

This reflects less on both men’s ultimate ambition than on the parlous position of their boss. Trump has been all over the place, policy-wise, since the Republicans lost their shirts in the midterm elections. For the first time, on issues such as immigration and Iran, he appears uncertain how to undo the damage without losing his base. Familiar hints that the election might have been rigged have been met with derision. Megyn Kelly, the conservative podcaster, posted: “Just stop.”

In short, Vance can’t talk, Rubio won’t, and Trump doesn’t know what to say.

news.title: Trump’s power is crumbling - and his billionaire allies are paying the price
news.text:
This is Dispatches with Patrick Cockburn, a subscriber-only newsletter from The i Paper. If you’d like to get this direct to your inbox, every single week, you can sign up here.

The scandal that led to the fall of Jensen Huang, the co-founder and boss of Nvidia, is superficially a simple tale of sex and allegations of espionage, but at a deeper level it is a symptom of the speed with which the political landscape is changing in America. 

Until his downfall, Huang appeared to tick all the right boxes for success and power in America. An autocrat at the heart of the AI and data centre revolution, commanding vast influence and wealth, he embodied the zeitgeist – the dominating spirit – of the Trumpian age in America.

In a single fortnight, two giant powers that until recently bestrode American and even world politics have been humbled, their invincibility exposed as a sham. One power is President Donald Trump, who led the Republican Party to calamitous defeat on 3 November. The other great power just diminished is Big Tech, which has seen its star performer at the head of Nvidia turned into something close to a political pariah. Put simply, Silicon Valley is not the power it was a week ago.

Flamboyant celebrity billionaires like Huang and Elon Musk are out of fashion. AI and data centres are increasingly viewed as dangerous innovations. Exit polls during the midterm elections showed 76 per cent of voters opposing the construction of a data centre in their community, while some 57 per cent saw AI as harmful to society as a whole. In the Republican stronghold of Texas, popular hostility to data centres was crucial to the Democrats’ unprecedented victory.

Trump had tried to save Huang whom he saw as a modern-day Henry Ford, doing for AI today what Ford had done for the car industry over a century ago. Their friendship was of recent vintage, but the Nvidia chief did not stint on flattery, saying: “America’s unique advantage is that no [other] country could possibly have its President Trump.” He contributed $25m to the construction of Trump’s favourite project, the new White House ballroom. Trump, for his part, saw AI as a possible route to reindustrialising America and Huang said that Nvidia might create $500bn AI infrastructure in the US.

Right up to the last moment, Trump was telling Huang to fight for his job, but by then the Nvidia chief was beset by enemies. China hawks inside and outside government were outraged by AI chip sales, directly and indirectly, to China by Nvidia and intelligence agencies had long been quietly antagonistic to Nvidia’s openness to trade with China.

Huang advocated selling AI chips to anybody who wanted to buy them, persuading Trump that it was in America’s interest that Beijing should depend on the United States for this essential component since otherwise China would develop its own advanced chips. As with many a Trump initiative, this one had a bizarre money-making element, with the federal government getting 15 per cent and later 25 per cent of sales revenue for certain AI models sold in China.

Supporters of Huang have mostly gone to ground, but earlier this week they were arguing that the “Deep State”, in the shape of the intelligence agencies and the foreign policy establishment, had long been looking for a means to bring down Huang – and they found one in his affair with businesswoman Alice Huang (no relation) who was an executive in a company called MegaSpeed in Singapore, importing AI chips from Nvidia worth some $4.6bn. US intelligence suspected these were being diverted to China, which could not buy them direct because of an export ban.

As the scandal broke, the New York Times and other papers revealed that unnamed US intelligence sources believed that Alice Huang was a spy working for Chinese intelligence to influence Jensen Huang. Beijing has denied that this is the case and the US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the justice department is yet to reach a conclusion on whether Alice Huang was a spy.

No details about this relationship were given and it seems a little strange that China should wish to influence the Nvidia chief who was already such a powerful influence in their favour in Washington. Alice Huang made no effort to conceal her relationship with Jensen Huang, which again seems peculiar if she was on a mission to obtain the secrets of Nvidia. Nevertheless, the media swiftly identified her as a Chinese Mata Hari, speaking glibly of a “honey trap” directed at Jensen Huang.

None of this is likely to do Alice Huang or Jensen Huang much good. Once labelled as a spy or the lover or associate of a spy, it is impossible to escape the taint of treachery. Politicians and public brought up on spy stories in books and films are credulous about what is leaked by intelligence agencies. This same is truer of the media which loves a good spy story, especially if it is spiced up with sex. The crucial question seldom asked in print or on air is why an intelligence agency is leaking some pieces of information? Aside from an innate love for truth and justice on the part of the leakers, what is their motive? Perhaps discrediting Jensen Huang and Nvidia as drivers of a relaxed US policy on high-tech trading with China.

Despite his friendship with Trump, Huang was a somewhat isolated figure in Washington, unpopular with the China hawks and foreign policy establishment. This did not much matter when Trump was at peak power over the last two years, but in the wake of midterm elections disastrous for the Republicans and a negative referendum on Trump himself, the President is visibly losing his power to protect his friends and allies. US bureaucracy and institutions long restive under the control of Trump’s weird underlings will leak more freely to reassert their control. Democrats with large majorities in both Houses of Congress will milk the Jensen Huang/Nvidia scandal mercilessly to discredit the administration.

But the fall of Jensen Huang and the chastening of Nvidia has an importance beyond the fate of a once powerful man and a huge company that retains immense influence. The power of Big Tech and Silicon Valley as a whole is weakened. Previously they had enjoyed a certain collective personality cult because of their vast wealth and technical prowess, but with their superstar Jensen Huang overthrown, their power is on the ebb. Big government will seek to reestablish its old authority and curb the Big Tech barons as over-mighty subjects who must be cut down to size.

Further Thoughts

Journalists prefer political victories to be decisive with clear-cut winners and losers because this makes for a simpler and more dramatic story. The Democratic Party triumph in the Congressional midterms on 3 November met this criteria far better than in most elections. For once, the transformational outcome of the poll is not being overstated. President Donald Trump’s aura of invincibility has evaporated overnight, though he still holds executive power and is fighting hard to avoid a self-fulfilling lame duck label.

His highly developed political instincts will have told him that it is best to counter-attack briskly after a defeat which explains his appointment of Stephen Miller, whose policies have in the past been described by some as far-right, authoritarian and ethno-nationalist, as his new White House chief of staff.

But a thumping historic defeat cannot be reversed whatever Trump’s tactics. The balance of power between him and his multitude of enemies has truly changed to their advantage and they smell blood in the water. Powerful Trump backers like Rupert Murdoch do not bet on losers: Fox News and the New York Post are already edging away from the President. Prior to the midterms any Republican Senator or Congressman not showing slavish obedience to Trump would inevitably be primaried out of politics by the Trump faithful. His iron grip on the Republican Party will be hard to break, even if it is weaker than before.

Everybody is pointing to Democrat success in right-wing bastions of the Deep South culminating in winning a Senate seat in Mississippi in the last few days. Democrats had already won in Texas, Georgia and South Carolina and come close in Florida and Louisiana. Divisions that have existed in American politics for 150 years are breaking down. In the 11 states of the Confederacy that seceded from the USA in 1861 and fought the Civil War – the legacy of which still underlies the greatest geographic divide in American politics – Democrats now hold Senate seats in six of them. 

Once, after the civil rights legislation in the 1960s, it was supposed that the deeply racist states of the South would become more like the North politically and culturally. But in practice over the last half century, the precise opposite happened. Liberal democracy was increasingly challenged in states like Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Michigan. The midterms saw what looks like this retrograde process abruptly going into reverse – perhaps permanently.

Another potential change gets too little mention: after their sweeping gains in the 2010 midterms, the Republicans systematically gerrymandered the national electoral system wherever they were in power to prevent a Democratic resurgence, regardless of the popular vote. This grossly undemocratic ploy worked fairly well until the midterms, but was overwhelmed by the Democratic wave. 

Another factor makes a successful Trump/Republican counter-attack more difficult. An essential component of Trump’s giant election victories was the Democratic Party’s dismal leadership since President Barack Obama left office in 2017. Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris were poor-quality politicians pushing a dead-in-the-water establishment agenda. This began to change with Zohran Mamdani’s successful campaign to be Mayor of New York in 2025, running relentlessly on an economic populist platform. In June this year, he told an interviewer with MS NOW: “The party, as a whole, has lost its focus on working people. People want to know, ‘What are you going to do for rent? What are you going to do for housing? What are you going to do for gas? What are you going to do for groceries?’ We have to have answers to that.”

Nothing attracts politicians of all stripes so much as a winning election formula which will see them win or retain office. Sincerely or opportunistically, a year later Democrat candidates were aping Mamdani.

Beneath the Radar

One of the most interesting questions post-midterms will be how far the emboldened Democrats avoid or repeat the multiple mistakes they have made over the past decade in fighting Donald Trump. Because they detested him so much, they concentrated all their fire on him to the exclusion of vote-winning policies. Despite two attempts to impeach Trump in his first term and multiple legal cases against him after he lost office, the Democrats never succeeded in landing a killer punch. On the contrary, they only succeeded in keeping Trump’s name at the top of the news agenda, forcing senior Republicans to rally around him, and giving him the status of a political martyr.

Democrats may have learned from past errors, which included being obsessed by the belief that they had been robbed of the presidency in 2016 by the machinations of President Vladimir Putin, a theory still believed by some though there is little evidence the election was stolen. For the true reasons for Democratic defeats, read any account of Hillary’s disastrous campaign.

Pursuit of allegations of corruption rather than impeachment of Trump is the better option. “We’re looking at the systemic corruption that has taken place,” the Maryland Democrat and likely chair of the House Judiciary Committee, Jamie Raskin, said in an interview with the Financial Times, “We’ve seen the most breathtaking and outrageous conflicts of interest pervade the Trump administration, beginning at the top.” (The White House denies that the Trump administration has any conflicts of interest. A White House spokesperson said: “As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people”.) He warned against being diverted by impeachment proceedings against Trump and instead urged focus on this “avalanche of corruption”.

Cockburn’s Picks

Estimable charities that once wholly depended on selfless volunteers have a sad tradition of being taken over by over-eager leaders and managers promoting unnecessary centralisation and re-organisation. This is apparently the grim fate threatening The Samaritans, the esteemed charity which since 1953 has provided phone support for people in acute mental distress and at risk of being suicidal. The volunteers manning the local hubs, where they sit together answering phone calls from deeply distressed people, are to be moved to larger buildings often far from where they live or, allegedly, they will operate from their home. The story has not been picked up very much by the media, but there is a lucid account of what is happening to The Samaritans by Justine Smith on The Private Eye Page 94 podcast.

news.title: Lauren Boebert Loses Colorado House Race to Democrat Eileen Laubacher
news.text:
Democrat Eileen Laubacher has unseated three-term Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) in a tightly contested race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.

The Associated Press called the race on Nov. 13 at 2:53 p.m. ET. With 99 percent of votes counted on Friday evening, Laubacher had received 48.8 percent of the vote to Boebert’s 47.9 percent.

Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris received 3.3 percent of the vote for the seat.

In a Nov. 13 post on X, Boebert said she called Laubacher to congratulate her. She also thanked God for sending her to serve Coloradoans.

“He sent me to serve,” she said. “My time to be sent to another unknown place is now.”

She also told her followers to stay tuned and that it wasn’t the last they would be hearing from her.

On Nov. 9, Boebert cautioned against declaring victory early and called for every ballot to be counted.

The Republican, once a strong ally of President Donald Trump, lost favor with the president as she sought reelection. Trump used social media to ask if anyone was interested in running against her.

The president threatened a primary challenge to Boebert in May after she campaigned for Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has opposed the Trump administration on issues such as the Iran war and budget deficits.

“Boebert is campaigning for the Worst ‘Republican’ Congressman ​in the History of our Country, Thomas Massie, of ​the Great Commonwealth of Kentucky, and anybody who can ⁠be that dumb deserves a good Primary fight!” Trump ​wrote on Truth Social.

Despite Trump’s rebuke, Boebert said she was not offended and would stand by Massie.

Massie lost his primary against Trump-endorsed Ed Gallrein, who won the 4th Congressional District seat in Kentucky over Democratic challenger Melissa Strange.

In 2020, Boebert unseated five-term incumbent Scott Tipton in a June primary before defeating Democrat Diane Mitsch Bush in the November 2020 general election.

Colorado’s 4th Congressional District was once a Republican stronghold. Trump previously won it by 18 points over Kamala Harris in 2024.

Laubacher is a retired two-star U.S. Navy rear admiral who served on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden.

Laubacher outraised Boebert in her bid for the congressional seat with $13.7 million to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

news.title: We Are Not Going Back
news.text:
Regret can be a nasty thing. Looking back on President Donald Trump’s first term and the first two years of his second term, the standard we apply, even if we don’t explicitly say it, centers on a simple question: Did the Trump years live up to their promise?

No matter what, we’ll still be asking this question once again in two years, win or lose the White House. A President Hillary Clinton would have been even more damaging to the country than the Barack Obama years. When Biden took his turn, he proved once again how much damage the Democrats can do in a short period of time. Kamala “Word Salad” Harris would have taken America to lows never before imagined.

The Democrat president of the United States wasn't capable of, and had no intention of, offering hope, leadership, or guidance. He offered depression, pessimism, and dire warnings to anyone who didn’t comply with his oppressive regime’s directives.

If the midterm results are any indication, that turned out to be a bad thing.

Now, here we sit, looking ahead at two years of performative, anti-American theatrics from Democrats in the House and Senate with a little jihad and socialist revolution thrown in. They want to take us back to the Biden years, where men and boys could say they were women and violate your daughter’s locker room and sports teams. For leftists, these were the glory years, and they were cut short. They now badly want to return to a time of social decay, rot, and bleakness. 

Since the 2026 midterms, a lot of conservatives are bummed, not just from the loss, but from the way Republicans lost. We realize now just how hollow and shallow are some of the Republican Party's "top" candidates and leaders. We realize that this buffer between us and Democrat rule has only two years left on his contract with America. We realize that some of those we thought might pick up Trump’s mantle of leadership are already starting to disappoint.

It’s at this low point that we may realize that the only solution to all of this is something that’s been literally staring us in the face this whole time.

It’s a mistake to put all your faith in one man, especially a man who’s term-limited and only human. You have to decide in your everyday life that we aren’t going back to the world the left gave us during the Obama and Biden years. You are the one who has to decide that you and we are not going to live under the terms the Democrats will try to hold over us the next two years.

This is not about resistance. We’re not resisting anything. We’re just not going backward. We're going forward one way or the other, and we're not going to cave. The Trump campaign’s “Make America Great Again” slogan has been more than a political slogan; it’s been a guiding mission that has framed a clear vision and objective for all of us. We’re not going back to a time where banks cancel our accounts because of our political views, and where the long arm of the government can order us to take an experimental injection or the Democrats in government will mandate that your employer fire you.

Your future, our future, doesn’t need to wait for 2028. It starts right now. It starts by deciding which movies and TV shows to watch and not watch; which games to watch on TV or in person; what to say online; what you buy and where you buy it; or whether or not you buy and carry that firearm. news.title: Colin Sheridan: Our politicians seem to have forgotten that Biden turned a blind eye to the murder of Palestinians
news.text:
In Ballina, Co Mayo in April 2023, Biden recalled the bricks his great-great-great-grandfather supplied for St Muredach’s Cathedral. His family’s migration to America belonged to the Famine years. He understood what an Irish audience would hear in that history. An inherited memory of state-sponsored hunger is a powerful thing to bring to a lectern. It ought to follow you back to the office.

By then, Biden had spent decades supporting Israel. In 1986, he called US assistance its best $3bn investment. Israel had occupied the Palestinian territories for 19 years. It had invaded and occupied southern Lebanon. It had illuminated the camps of Sabra and Shatila in West Beirut, allowing the militias it armed and supported to carry out the massacres. Some investment.

Four years earlier, Ronald Reagan had telephoned Menachem Begin about the bombardment of the Lebanese capital. His diary recorded his horror at a photograph of a baby with its arms blown off, and his warning that the relationship between the two countries was endangered. 

The child had lost both arms. The president had found something to put in his diary. There is a familiar vanity in these accounts. The powerful man invites us into the room where he wrestled with his conscience. Somewhere outside are the people whose suffering provides the occasion for this demonstration of presidential depth.

In 2016, with Biden as vice-president, the Obama administration pledged $38bn in military assistance over 10 years. Gaza was under blockade. That February alone, Israel demolished or dismantled 237 Palestinian homes and livelihood structures in the West Bank, displacing 330 people, half of them children. Washington had ample information and historical evidence about the country receiving its money.

Then came October 7, 2023. In its immediate aftermath Biden spoke of seeing confirmed pictures of terrorists beheading children. His administration subsequently clarified that neither he nor it had seen those pictures or independently confirmed the reports. 

 He had supplied presidential authority to something he did not know. Imagine how many were killed as a result

On October 25, asked about Palestinian deaths, he questioned whether Palestinians were telling the truth about the numbers. His response to innocent deaths was they were “the price of waging a war”.

Consider the distribution of his scepticism. An unverified account of atrocities against Israelis — since disproven — acquired his wholehearted endorsement. Palestinian accounts of their dead encountered his snark.

On December 9, his administration invoked emergency authority to bypass the usual congressional review for a proposed tank-ammunition sale. Two days later, Biden reiterated his identification as a Zionist. The following day, he described Israel’s bombing as indiscriminate. Three decisions, four days, one president.

We watched Gaza burn on screens. Consider the evidence a president “wrestling with his conscience” could summon. Intelligence assessments. Satellite imagery. Diplomats and military officers to explain what Israel was doing and what America was supporting. Then consider the generosity required to imagine that we understood something beyond his comprehension.

By March 2024, international experts were warning of imminent famine in northern Gaza. Famine, remember that Joe! In May, Biden acknowledged that American bombs had killed civilians. His administration paused a shipment over concerns about Rafah. He knew enough to identify the danger and demonstrate that he could interrupt the supply. ProPublica reported that two US government bodies concluded Israel deliberately obstructed aid. Former US secretary of state Antony Blinken rejected their findings.

Defence of the indefensible

Yet when the International Criminal Court prosecutor sought warrants for Israeli leaders in May, Biden called the application “outrageous”. When judges issued warrants in November, finding reasonable grounds for charges including starvation as a method of warfare, he called those outrageous too. He was using his office to defend the men the court sought to hold accountable.

Meanwhile, students demanding a change in American policy received a lecture about decorum. On May 2, Biden defended peaceful protest and condemned violence and disruption. Asked whether the demonstrations had prompted him to reconsider his regional policies, he answered, “No.” They were entitled to be heard. He had already decided what hearing them would change. Nothing.

In August, Kamala Harris told protesters interrupting her Michigan rally: “If you want Donald Trump to win, then say that.” Her message was clear: whatever genocide your tax dollars are paying for, consider the alternative and shut-the-fuck-up.

In January, days before Trump took office, Biden’s administration celebrated its role in negotiating another failed ceasefire. It also proposed an $8bn arms sale that month. Both belong in the account of his final weeks. So do his “warnings" to Netanyahu, including his explicit statement in April that American policy would depend on Israeli action to protect civilians. His administration understood that support could carry conditions. It said so. It did nothing.

Let the memoirs record every furious telephone call. Let Hunter describe every private anguish he claims his father felt. Nobody in his circle seems intent on holding him responsible for having the knowledge he had of what American weapons were doing, and the decades-old experience of how Israel would wield that power. He continued supplying them and defending Israel against accountability. 

 He ran and got elected on the reputation of the grand old statesman. He knew what he was doing.

In Ballina, he knew, too, how to make a family’s experience of state-sponsored hunger matter. In office, he had the power to end another people’s hunger. He had the power to put food in their hands and mouths. He repeatedly, intentionally, chose another way.

Our political leaders can have their photgraphs with him. Just let them remember that the Palestinians they claim to so passionately support have had to live — and die — with his decisions.
news.summary: Former US president has spent decades supporting Israel — so why should he not be held accountable for atrocities when visiting our country?
